title: NestJS at scale — variant 2
description: Ride-sharing, telehealth, claims and pharmacy: global-module sprawl, transient vs request scope, discovery, lazy modules, Kafka reply partitions, RMQ acks, shutdown ordering and esbuild in tests.

domains.name: Testing seams, hexagonal structure and builds

questions.stem: A ride-sharing monolith has 70 modules, and over the years developers marked 45 of them `@Global()` to avoid import errors. Leadership wants to carve out Pricing and Dispatch as separate services within a year, but nobody can tell from the code which modules Pricing actually uses. What module policy should the team adopt?

options.text: Global only for infrastructure; feature modules export a facade and are imported explicitly
options.why: Explicit imports make the dependency graph readable from the code, which is exactly the map needed to cut a service out.

options.text: Mark the remaining 25 modules `@Global()` too, so the policy is at least consistent
options.why: Consistent, but it erases the graph entirely; every provider can reach every other, so an extraction has no visible seam.

options.text: Collect all shared providers into one `SharedModule` that every feature module imports
options.why: It replaces 45 hidden edges with one god module that everything depends on, which is just as hard to split.

options.text: Split every module into its own npm package now so boundaries are enforced by the package manager
options.why: It enforces boundaries, but with versioning and release overhead for 70 packages long before anyone knows which seams matter.

questions.explain: Imports are documentation of coupling. Reserve global modules for cross-cutting infrastructure; everything else should be imported where it is used, so the module tree shows the seams you will later cut along.

questions.stem: A telehealth API wants every log line to carry the name of the class that wrote it. A developer made `AppLogger` `Scope.REQUEST` so each class could call `setContext(ClassName)` on its own copy. Within a week, 180 providers became request-scoped and the API's throughput dropped by a third. Which scope gives each class its own logger without that cost?

options.text: `Scope.DEFAULT`, calling `setContext()` before every log call
options.why: One shared instance means concurrent requests overwrite each other's context, so lines get the wrong class name.

options.text: `Scope.TRANSIENT`
options.why: Each consumer gets its own instance at bootstrap, and transient scope does not bubble to the consumers, so they stay singletons.

options.text: `Scope.REQUEST` with `durable: true`
options.why: Durable trees are keyed by a context strategy such as tenant, not by class; it would still be shared across classes and adds a context strategy for no reason.

options.text: Keep `Scope.REQUEST` but inject it only into controllers
options.why: Request scope still bubbles up from every service that logs, and services are where most log lines come from.

questions.explain: Pick the scope by what varies: per consumer is transient, per request is request (and it bubbles to everything above it). Per-consumer state such as a logger context never needs request scope.

questions.stem: An insurance claims platform handles 25 claim types, each with its own handler class, and separate teams add new types in their own modules several times a quarter. Today a central `ClaimRouter` injects all 25 handlers in its constructor and has a `switch`. Teams keep conflicting on that file. Which design lets a team add a claim type without touching shared code, while failing fast at startup if two handlers claim the same type?

options.text: Look the handler up by naming convention per request with `ModuleRef.get(`${type}Handler`, { strict: false })`
options.why: No central file, but a typo or missing handler only fails when that claim type is first submitted, and `strict: false` reaches across module boundaries.

options.text: A `@ClaimHandler('motor')` decorator plus `DiscoveryService` building the map at bootstrap
options.why: Teams only decorate their class; discovery runs at bootstrap, so duplicates or gaps are detected before the app takes traffic.

options.text: Keep the constructor injection but split the `switch` into one file per team
options.why: The constructor still lists every handler, so the conflicts move rather than disappear.

options.text: Create a new handler instance per claim with `moduleRef.create(HandlerClass)`
options.why: It still needs a central type-to-class map, and building a fresh instance per claim adds allocation and loses any warmed state.

questions.explain: For plugin-style extension inside one Nest app, mark classes with metadata and discover them once at bootstrap. Resolving by string at request time moves wiring errors from startup to production traffic.

questions.stem: A logistics codebase, compiled to CommonJS, uses an `index.ts` barrel in every folder. After a refactor, startup fails with "Nest can't resolve dependencies of the RoutePlanner (?). Please make sure that the argument at index [0] is available in the current module". The dependency is a plain singleton in the same module, and it is clearly listed in `providers`. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The provider must also be added to the module's `exports`
options.why: Exports matter only for other modules; a provider is always injectable inside its own module.

options.text: `RoutePlanner` needs `Scope.TRANSIENT` to be created after its dependency
options.why: Scope doesn't control creation order for singletons, and this error is about an unknown token, not timing.

options.text: A barrel import cycle left the class `undefined` when its metadata was emitted
options.why: With a cycle, one module's exports are not yet initialised when the other evaluates its decorators, so Nest sees `undefined` as the parameter type.

options.text: The module needs `@Global()` so the dependency is visible during bootstrap
options.why: Visibility isn't the issue inside one module; making it global would not change an `undefined` type at index 0.

questions.explain: A `?` in Nest's dependency error often means the type was `undefined` when TypeScript emitted metadata, typically because of a circular file import, which barrel files make easy to create. Fix the file graph; `forwardRef` is for genuine provider cycles.

questions.stem: A reporting Lambda boots a Nest app of 120 modules; cold starts take 3.5 s, and the product team wants p95 under 1.5 s. Each invocation path uses only one of `ReportsModule` or `ExportModule`, the heavy modules. Budget rules out provisioned concurrency. What should change?

options.text: Increase Lambda memory to 3 GB so module initialisation runs on more CPU
options.why: It shaves time off boot at a higher per-ms price, but still initialises 120 modules on every cold start.

options.text: Recreate the Nest app inside every invocation so no stale state leaks between requests
options.why: That pays the full bootstrap on every request, not only cold starts, making latency far worse.

options.text: A slim root module, the app cached across invocations, heavy modules via `LazyModuleLoader`
options.why: Cold start only builds what every path needs; the heavy module's cost is paid once per container, and only on the path that uses it.

options.text: Mark all heavy modules `@Global()` so they are resolved once and shared
options.why: Global modules are still instantiated at bootstrap, so the cold start doesn't get shorter.

questions.explain: In serverless, startup cost is paid per container. Keep the root module small, reuse the app across invocations, and lazy-load modules that only some paths need.

questions.stem: A public booking API runs 12 replicas behind a load balancer and uses `@nestjs/throttler` with the default in-memory storage at 100 requests per minute per API key. A partner is observed sending around 1,100 requests per minute without being throttled. Autoscaling moves between 6 and 30 replicas. What should the team do?

options.text: Divide the limit by the replica count and set it to 8 per minute
options.why: It only holds at exactly 12 replicas and even load-balancing; at 6 replicas partners get half their quota, at 30 they get more than double.

options.text: Give the throttler a shared storage such as Redis
options.why: One counter per key across the fleet keeps the limit correct at any replica count.

options.text: Enable sticky sessions so each API key always lands on the same replica
options.why: It roughly fixes counting, but uneven key sizes create hot replicas, and every scale event or pod restart reshuffles keys.

options.text: Move the throttling logic from a guard into an interceptor so it runs later
options.why: Running later doesn't change the fact that each replica keeps its own counter; it also lets work start before the limit is checked.

questions.explain: Any in-memory limiter, cache or lock is per process. Once you scale horizontally, state that must be global, such as a rate budget, needs a shared store.

questions.stem: A healthcare portal uses a global `ClassSerializerInterceptor`, and `UserEntity` marks `passwordHash` with `@Exclude()`. A developer added a CSV-style export endpoint that injects `@Res() res` to set a `Content-Disposition` header, then calls `res.json(users)`. Security review finds password hashes in the export. What is the correct change?

options.text: Add `@Exclude()` to `passwordHash` in a second DTO used only by the export
options.why: The entity already excludes it; the serializer never ran, so another decorator would also be ignored.

options.text: Add `select: false` to the column and keep the handler as it is
options.why: That hides this one field, but every other future `@Exclude()` would still be bypassed on this endpoint.

options.text: Use `@Res({ passthrough: true })` or `@Header()`, and return the users
options.why: With passthrough Nest still owns the response, so interceptors run on the returned value and `@Exclude()` applies.

options.text: Call `JSON.stringify(users)` before `res.send()` so class-transformer rules are honoured
options.why: Plain `JSON.stringify` knows nothing about class-transformer decorators, so it serializes the hash too.

questions.explain: Injecting `@Res()` takes the response away from Nest: interceptors no longer transform what you return, so serialization and envelopes are bypassed. Use passthrough or `@Header()` and return values.

questions.stem: A warehouse client uploads stock counts as a JSON array of up to 5,000 items to `@Post('counts') upsert(@Body() items: StockCountDto[])`. A global `ValidationPipe` is configured with `whitelist: true, transform: true`. Yesterday a batch with negative quantities and missing SKUs was accepted and corrupted inventory. What should change?

options.text: Add `forbidNonWhitelisted: true` to the global pipe
options.why: It rejects unknown properties, but the items are never validated against the DTO at all, so negative quantities still pass.

options.text: Use `@Body(new ParseArrayPipe({ items: StockCountDto }))`
options.why: TypeScript erases the array's element type, so the global pipe cannot know the item class; `ParseArrayPipe` validates each element.

options.text: Enable `transformOptions: { enableImplicitConversion: true }`
options.why: It converts primitives, but still has no element class to convert to, and it brings its own trap of turning `"false"` into `true`.

options.text: Validate in the service with a loop of `if` checks before the upsert
options.why: It works, but duplicates the DTO rules in a second place and returns 500-style errors instead of a structured 400.

questions.explain: The validation pipe can only use the runtime metatype it receives. Arrays, generics and interfaces lose their element type at compile time, so declare it explicitly (`ParseArrayPipe`, or a wrapper DTO with `@ValidateNested({ each: true })` and `@Type`).

questions.stem: A pharmacy app runs a hybrid Nest app: HTTP plus NATS handlers for internal calls, which must also be authenticated with a service token. A global `AuthGuard` reads `context.switchToHttp().getRequest().headers.authorization`. Since NATS handlers were added, every internal call fails with a 500 `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`. What fix keeps one guard and protects both transports?

options.text: Branch on `context.getType()` and read the token from the RPC context for `'rpc'`
options.why: `ExecutionContext` is transport-neutral; asking for the type first lets one guard read credentials from the right place.

options.text: Mark every NATS handler `@Public()` so the guard skips them
options.why: It stops the crash by turning off authentication for internal calls, which the requirement forbids.

options.text: Authenticate NATS calls in an Express middleware before they reach the handler
options.why: Middleware runs only in the HTTP adapter; NATS messages never pass through it.

options.text: Split the hybrid app into two deployments with separate guard classes
options.why: It works, but doubles deployments and duplicates the auth logic to fix a branch that fits in one guard.

questions.explain: Guards, interceptors and filters receive an `ExecutionContext`/`ArgumentsHost` that can be HTTP, RPC or WebSocket. Shared enhancers must check `getType()` before switching to a transport-specific view.

questions.stem: A ride-pricing gateway uses Nest's Kafka client for request-reply: `send('price.quote', ...)` with `subscribeToResponseOf('price.quote')` before `connect()`. It worked with 3 pods. After scaling to 12 pods for a holiday, about two thirds of the pods fail every quote at once with "The client consumer did not subscribe to the corresponding reply topic", while the pricing service is healthy. The topic `price.quote.reply` has 4 partitions. What is the fix?

options.text: Add `timeout(10000)` to the `send()` pipeline so slow replies are tolerated
options.why: Nothing is slow; those pods fail before sending because they own no reply partition, so a timeout never comes into play.

options.text: Raise the pricing service's consumer concurrency so it answers faster
options.why: Pricing is healthy; the failing pods cannot even send a request because they have no reply partition.

options.text: Give `price.quote.reply` at least as many partitions as gateway pods
options.why: Each client instance must own at least one reply partition; with 12 pods and 4 partitions, eight pods have none, so Nest refuses to send their requests.

options.text: Give each gateway pod its own consumer `groupId` so that every pod reads every partition of the reply topic
options.why: Every pod then reads every reply, including other pods' replies, which wastes throughput, and the routing by partition no longer matches.

questions.explain: Nest's Kafka request-reply routes replies by partition: every client instance needs its own reply partition. Size reply topics for peak pod count, or use HTTP/gRPC for synchronous calls and keep Kafka for events.

questions.stem: A trip service emits `trip.events` (requested, accepted, completed) through a Nest `ClientKafka` with `this.kafka.emit('trip.events', event)`. The billing consumer, running 8 instances, sometimes processes `completed` before `accepted` for the same trip and computes no fare. What should the producer change?

options.text: Emit `{ key: event.tripId, value: event }` so all events of a trip land on one partition
options.why: Kafka orders messages only within a partition; keying by trip keeps each trip's events in order for the consumer.

options.text: Reduce the topic to one partition
options.why: It guarantees order, but caps billing at one consumer and one partition's throughput.

options.text: Switch from `emit()` to `send()` so each event waits for an acknowledgement
options.why: Request-reply adds a reply topic and latency per event; without a key the events still spread across partitions.

options.text: Have billing buffer events and sort them by timestamp before processing
options.why: It works sometimes, but clocks differ between producers and the buffer window is a guess; late events still break it.

questions.explain: Ordering in Kafka is per partition, and the partition is chosen by the key. Key by the entity whose events must stay ordered; Nest's Kafka client accepts `{ key, value, headers }`.

questions.stem: A claims service uses `@nestjs/cqrs`. After `ApproveClaimHandler` commits the approval to Postgres it publishes `ClaimApproved` on the `EventBus`; an event handler calls the payments API to pay out. Twice this month a pod was OOM-killed between commit and payout, and those claims stayed approved but unpaid. Which design closes that gap?

options.text: Move the payout into a CQRS saga that maps `ClaimApproved` to a `PayOutClaim` command
options.why: Sagas are RxJS streams in the same process; a crash still loses the event between commit and command.

options.text: Write the event to an outbox table in the approval's transaction; a relay delivers it
options.why: The event is durable the moment the approval is, so a crash only delays the payout; the payout side must be idempotent.

options.text: Wrap the event handler's API call in three retries with backoff
options.why: Retries help with flaky APIs but not with a process that died; the in-memory event is gone.

options.text: Publish `ClaimApproved` to Kafka right after the database commit instead of to the `EventBus`
options.why: It is still a dual write: a crash between commit and publish loses the event exactly as before.

questions.explain: By default the CQRS module's `EventBus` publishes in process, from memory. Anything that must survive a crash needs the event persisted atomically with the state change, typically with a transactional outbox; Nest 12's docs add an `@nestjs/outbox` package for exactly this.

questions.stem: An airline's baggage service consumes `bag.scanned` from RabbitMQ with Nest's RMQ transport using default options. Handlers write to a slow tracking API that takes up to 8 s. During a memory leak incident, 14 pods were OOM-killed and about 600 scans disappeared: not in the tracking API, not in the queue. Which change makes a crash mid-handler safe?

options.text: `noAck: false`, and ack via `RmqContext` after the API write
options.why: With manual acknowledgement RabbitMQ keeps the message until the handler acks it, so a crashed pod's in-flight messages are redelivered.

options.text: Make the queue durable with `queueOptions: { durable: true }`
options.why: Durability keeps queued messages across broker restarts, but with auto-ack the in-flight message was already removed when the pod received it.

options.text: Raise `prefetchCount` so each pod holds more messages and finishes faster
options.why: More prefetched messages under auto-ack means more messages lost when a pod dies.

options.text: Move the RMQ handler from `@EventPattern` to `@MessagePattern`
options.why: That changes the interaction to request-reply; the acknowledgement mode is the same.

questions.explain: With auto-ack, delivery is the acknowledgement: a crash loses everything in flight. Acknowledge only after the side effect is done, and make the handler idempotent because redelivery will happen.

questions.stem: A fraud-scoring API warms a 2 GB model and rule cache from S3 in an async `useFactory` provider. Bootstrap takes 4 minutes, and the Kubernetes liveness probe (initial delay 60 s) restarts pods in a loop during rollouts. Traffic must not reach a pod until the cache is warm. What should change?

options.text: Raise the liveness probe's initial delay to 5 minutes
options.why: It stops the loop, but also delays detection of real hangs at every start and lets a stuck pod sit for 5 minutes.

options.text: Move the warm-up into `onModuleInit` so it runs after the providers are built
options.why: Nest awaits `onModuleInit` during bootstrap too, so the server still doesn't listen for 4 minutes.

options.text: Serve traffic immediately and warm each cache entry lazily on first use
options.why: Pods take traffic before they can score fraud, so early requests time out or are scored without rules.

options.text: Listen first and warm in the background, with a `startupProbe` and a readiness check that fails until warm
options.why: Liveness sees a live process, readiness keeps traffic away until the cache is ready, and the startup probe gives a bounded window.

questions.explain: Separate 'alive' from 'ready'. Long warm-ups should not block the event loop or bootstrap; expose readiness through a health check (for example with Terminus) and let the platform route traffic only when ready.

questions.stem: On Nest 12, an `AuditBuffer` service in `AuditModule` injects `DatabaseService` from `DatabaseModule`, which `AuditModule` imports, and flushes buffered rows in its `onModuleDestroy`. `DatabaseService` closes its pool in its own `onModuleDestroy`. A developer had added a 2-second `setTimeout` before the pool close because flushes failed with 'pool is closed' on Nest 9. What should the team do now?

options.text: Keep the timeout, because Nest still runs destroy hooks in module registration order
options.why: That was the old behaviour; Nest 11 changed the termination order.

options.text: Remove the timeout: since Nest 11 an imported module is terminated after the modules that import it
options.why: `AuditModule` imports `DatabaseModule`, so its `onModuleDestroy` runs first and the pool closes after the flush.

options.text: Move the flush into `beforeApplicationShutdown` so it runs after every destroy hook
options.why: It runs after all `onModuleDestroy` hooks, which is after the pool has closed, so the flush would always fail.

options.text: Make `DatabaseModule` `@Global()` so it is destroyed last
options.why: Global modules are destroyed late, but the import of `DatabaseModule` already guarantees this order, so global adds nothing.

questions.explain: Since Nest 11, termination hooks run in the reverse of init order, module by module: imported modules are initialised first and destroyed last. Nest 12 keeps that and also orders providers inside one module by dependency level. Express ordering through module imports, not through sleeps.

questions.stem: A Nest API behind an AWS ALB on Kubernetes has `enableShutdownHooks()` on and drains in-flight requests correctly. Still, every rollout produces a burst of 502s in the first few seconds after a pod receives SIGTERM: the ALB keeps sending new requests to a pod whose server has already closed. What fixes the 502s?

options.text: Raise `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` from 30 to 120
options.why: More time after SIGTERM doesn't help; the server closes promptly and new requests still arrive at it.

options.text: A `preStop` sleep so the pod leaves the target group before SIGTERM
options.why: Endpoint removal propagates to the load balancer asynchronously; delaying SIGTERM lets routing catch up before the server stops accepting.

options.text: Close the HTTP server earlier, in `onModuleDestroy`, to fail fast
options.why: Closing sooner makes the window during which the ALB hits a closed server longer, not shorter.

options.text: Tighten ALB health checks to every 5 seconds with an unhealthy threshold of 2
options.why: Faster health checks shrink the window a little, but deregistration still lags behind SIGTERM.

questions.explain: Graceful shutdown has two halves: stop new traffic (deregistration, readiness, a preStop delay) and finish old traffic (drain in-flight requests in Nest's shutdown hooks). Nest's hooks only cover the second half, because the platform controls routing.

questions.stem: A media team moves its Nest unit tests from Jest with `ts-jest` to Vitest (on Vite 7) for speed. Suddenly every service built through `Test.createTestingModule` has `undefined` dependencies, although nothing else changed. What is the fix?

options.text: Add `import 'reflect-metadata'` to the Vitest setup file
options.why: The polyfill is needed, but the problem is that the metadata it would read was never emitted.

options.text: Use the SWC plugin for Vitest (`unplugin-swc`) so decorator metadata is emitted
options.why: On Vite 7 Vitest transforms TypeScript with esbuild, which drops decorator metadata (Vite 8's Oxc supports it only partly); SWC emits it.

options.text: Replace every constructor injection with `moduleRef.get()` calls in `onModuleInit`
options.why: It works around the symptom by giving up constructor injection across the codebase.

options.text: Run the tests against the compiled `dist/` output instead of the sources
options.why: It would work if `tsc` built `dist`, but you lose fast source-mapped test runs, which was the point of switching.

questions.explain: Nest's type-based DI depends on `design:paramtypes`. Any esbuild-based toolchain (tsx, Vitest on Vite 7, many bundlers) drops it; use SWC or `tsc` wherever Nest code is compiled.

questions.stem: A ticket-resale API calls `app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, forbidNonWhitelisted: true }))` in `main.ts`. A new e2e test builds the app from `AppModule` via `Test.createTestingModule` and expects 400 for an unknown field, but gets 201. A teammate proposes adding the same `useGlobalPipes` call to the test setup. What do you recommend instead?

options.text: Accept the teammate's change, since it is a single line in the test helper
options.why: It passes the test by duplicating configuration, and the next difference between `main.ts` and the helper goes unnoticed.

options.text: Test validation only in unit tests of the DTO classes
options.why: DTO unit tests prove the decorators, not that the running app applies them, which is exactly what broke.

options.text: Register the pipe as `{ provide: APP_PIPE, useValue: new ValidationPipe({...}) }` in `AppModule`
options.why: The pipe becomes part of the module tree, so production, tests and other entry points all build it the same way.

options.text: Start the real `main.ts` in a child process for every e2e test
options.why: It tests the real wiring, but makes each test pay a full process start and loses provider overrides.

questions.explain: Configuration in `main.ts` is invisible to everything that builds the app from modules. Register global pipes, guards, interceptors and filters with the `APP_*` tokens.

questions.stem: In a wallet service built with ports and adapters, the `TransferFunds` use case debits one account, credits another and writes an outbox row. Repositories are TypeORM adapters injected into the use case. A developer wrapped the use case body in `this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => { ... })` but still calls the injected repositories; a forced error after the debit leaves the debit in place. Which design keeps the domain free of ORM types and makes the three writes atomic?

options.text: Inject `DataSource` into the use case and call `manager.getRepository(...)` for each write
options.why: It is atomic, but the use case now depends on TypeORM, which defeats the ports-and-adapters boundary.

options.text: A `UnitOfWork` port whose adapter keeps the transaction in async context for the repositories
options.why: The use case only calls `uow.run(...)`, and every repository write inside joins the same transaction; this is what `@nestjs-cls/transactional` provides.

options.text: Have each repository open its own transaction around its write
options.why: Each write commits on its own, so a failure after the debit still leaves it committed.

options.text: Keep the code and add a compensating credit in a `catch` block
options.why: Compensation can itself fail or race with readers who already saw the debit; it is not a substitute for a local transaction.

questions.explain: Only queries issued through the transaction's manager (or `tx` in Prisma) are inside it. In hexagonal code, model the transaction boundary as a port and let adapters pick up the active transaction from context.

questions.stem: A Nest worker for a retail chain, created with `NestFactory.createMicroservice`, is bundled with esbuild to shrink its image from 400 MB to 60 MB. To keep DI working without decorator metadata, the team added an explicit `@Inject(Token)` to every constructor parameter. Injection now works, but a `@MessagePattern` handler that takes `@Payload() dto: RestockDto` accepts invalid payloads, although a global `ValidationPipe` is registered with `APP_PIPE`. Why?

options.text: `ValidationPipe` does not run for microservice handlers at all
options.why: Pipes run for RPC handlers too, and this one is bound in the worker's module tree; the problem is what it receives.

options.text: `@Payload()` bypasses pipes unless `transform: true` is set
options.why: Transform controls whether the converted object replaces the input; it does not decide whether validation runs.

options.text: The pipe must also be registered with `useGlobalPipes` on the microservice instance
options.why: `APP_PIPE` already binds it in the module tree; adding another registration does not give it the missing type.

options.text: Without emitted metadata the pipe gets no parameter class, so it skips validation
options.why: `@Inject` only fixes constructor parameters; handler parameter types still come from emitted metadata, which esbuild dropped.

questions.explain: Decorator metadata is used in more places than constructors: validation and transformation pipes read handler parameter types too. Silent loss of validation is the dangerous symptom of an esbuild build; compile with `tsc` or SWC.
